items.title: Vandemataram Movement & Home Rule in Andhra
items.body:
**In one line** — This is the earliest 'awakening' phase of the freedom struggle in Andhra (about 1905 to 1916), when Telugu students, writers and strongmen first turned against British rule.

**Why it is asked** — APPSC loves to ask who did what first: the trigger of the Vandemataram stir, Bipin Chandra Pal's tour, the first political prisoner, and the two Home Rule Leagues.

## The story

- **Cause:** In 1905 the British split Bengal into two provinces (the **Partition of Bengal**). Indians saw this as 'divide and rule', and anger spread across the country as the **Swadeshi movement** — 'use our own goods, boycott British goods'. ('Swadeshi' means 'of one's own country'.)
- **What happened in Andhra (1905–07):** the wave reached Andhra towns as the **Vandemataram agitation** ('Vande Mataram' = 'I bow to you, Mother [India]', a patriotic cry). Students in **Rajahmundry** and other towns took up Swadeshi, boycott of foreign cloth, and national education.
- The extremist leader **Bipin Chandra Pal** toured the region in **1907** (including Rajahmundry) and fired up the youth. ('Extremist' here means leaders who wanted bolder, direct action, not just polite petitions.)
- **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** wrote a strong article against the British, was tried for **sedition** (writing/speaking to excite revolt against the government) and jailed — one of Andhra's **earliest political prisoners**.
- **Kodi Rammurthy Naidu**, a famous Telugu **wrestler and strongman**, performed astonishing feats of strength that made Indians feel proud and strong at a time when British rule made them feel weak — so he became a living **symbol of national self-confidence**.
- **Result:** these years built the first base of nationalist feeling in Andhra, which the next phase organised.

## Home Rule Movement (1916)

- 'Home Rule' means **self-government within the British Empire** (run our own affairs, but stay in the Empire for now).
- Two **Home Rule Leagues** were started in 1916 — **Bal Gangadhar Tilak's** (April) and **Annie Besant's** (September). Besant's League was active across the **Madras Presidency**, including Andhra.
- **Why it matters:** it created local branches and trained workers — the very network Gandhi later used for Non-Cooperation.

## Picture it (timeline)

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1905 | Partition of Bengal → Swadeshi begins |
| 1905–07 | Vandemataram agitation in Andhra |
| 1907 | Bipin Chandra Pal's tour (Rajahmundry) |
| 1916 | Home Rule Leagues (Tilak, Besant) reach Andhra |

## Terms explained

- **Swadeshi** — using and promoting goods made in one's own country, boycotting foreign goods.
- **Sedition** — speech or writing meant to stir up revolt against the government; a jailable offence under the British.
- **Extremist** — a nationalist who favoured bold, direct action over moderate petitioning.
- **Home Rule** — self-government within the British Empire.

**Don't confuse** — the **Vandemataram/Swadeshi phase (1905–07)** was an *Extremist, boycott* movement, NOT a moderate 'petition-only' phase. Also keep **Home Rule (1916, constitutional)** separate from the later armed Rampa revolt.

**Remember it** — 'Partition (1905) lit the spark; Pal fanned it (1907); Home Rule organised it (1916).'

**TL;DR**

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Partition of Bengal, 1905 |
| Andhra phase | Vandemataram, 1905–07 |
| Fired up youth | Bipin Chandra Pal, 1907 (Rajahmundry) |
| Early prisoner | Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao (sedition) |
| Strongman symbol | Kodi Rammurthy Naidu |
| Home Rule 1916 | Tilak (April) & Annie Besant (September) |
keyPoints: Vandemataram/Swadeshi agitation in Andhra (1905–07) followed the 1905 Partition of Bengal.
Bipin Chandra Pal's 1907 tour (incl. Rajahmundry) roused Andhra youth to Swadeshi and boycott.
Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao was jailed for sedition — an early Andhra political prisoner.
Kodi Rammurthy Naidu, strongman/wrestler, symbolised Indian strength and national pride.
Home Rule Leagues (1916): Tilak (April) and Annie Besant (September) demanded self-government.

items.title: Non-Cooperation Movement in Andhra (1920–22)
items.body:
**In one line** — This is Gandhi's first all-India mass movement (1920–22), and in Andhra it became a powerful peasants' revolt against taxes, liquor and British institutions.

**Why it is asked** — The three famous Andhra episodes (Chirala–Perala, Pedanandipadu, Palnadu) and their leaders are repeat APPSC favourites, often as match-the-pairs.

## The story

- **Cause:** after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) and the Khilafat issue, Gandhi called for **Non-Cooperation** — Indians would simply *stop cooperating* with British rule: boycott courts, councils, schools and foreign cloth, give up titles, and refuse unjust taxes.
- **What happened in Andhra:** the districts of **Guntur, Krishna and Palnadu** became one of the most active regions of the whole **Madras Presidency** (the big British province that then included Andhra). The movement took the shape of **no-tax (no-revenue) satyagrahas**, picketing of **toddy (liquor) shops**, and boycott of courts and councils.
- ('Satyagraha' = Gandhi's method of non-violent, truthful resistance — literally 'holding firmly to truth'.)
- **Result:** these local struggles gave the Congress deep roots in Andhra villages. The whole movement was called off nationally after the violent **Chauri Chaura** incident (February 1922), where a mob burned a police station.

## The three Andhra episodes

| Episode (year) | Place / district | What made it special | Leader |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chirala–Perala satyagraha (1921) | Guntur district | Townspeople left their homes and lived in a hut-camp named **Ramnagar** for about 11 months to avoid paying higher municipal taxes | **Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya** ('Andhra Ratna') |
| Pedanandipadu campaign (1921–22) | Guntur district | A **no-revenue (no-tax) satyagraha** — peasants refused to pay land revenue | **Parvataneni Veerayya Choudary**, guided by Konda Venkatappayya |
| Palnadu forest satyagraha (1921–22) | Palnadu, Guntur | Peasants defied the **Pullari (grazing) tax** and forest rules; the leader was **shot dead in 1922** | **Kanneganti Hanumanthu** |

## Terms explained

- **Satyagraha** — Gandhi's non-violent resistance based on truth and moral force.
- **No-revenue / no-tax satyagraha** — organised refusal by farmers to pay land revenue to the government.
- **Pullari tax** — a tax on grazing cattle and using forest produce.
- **Picketing** — standing peacefully outside a shop (here, liquor shops) to persuade people not to use it.

**Don't confuse** — the Gandhian, **non-violent Non-Cooperation** campaigns are different from the **armed Rampa Rebellion** of Alluri Sitarama Raju (same years, but a separate tribal revolt).

**Remember it** — 'Three C-P-P towns of Guntur: **C**hirala–Perala (exodus), **P**edanandipadu (no-tax), **P**alnadu (grazing-tax martyr).'

**TL;DR**

- Non-Cooperation (1920–22): boycott courts/councils/schools/foreign cloth, no-tax, give up titles.
- Strongest in Guntur, Krishna, Palnadu.
- Chirala–Perala → Ramnagar exodus (Duggirala); Pedanandipadu → no-tax (Parvataneni); Palnadu → Pullari-tax martyr (Kanneganti).
- Called off nationally after Chauri Chaura (Feb 1922).
keyPoints: Non-Cooperation (1920–22) was strongest in Guntur, Krishna and Palnadu in Andhra.
Chirala–Perala (1921): people vacated the towns and lived in 'Ramnagar' under Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya.
Pedanandipadu (Guntur): no-revenue satyagraha led by Parvataneni Veerayya Choudary.
Palnadu: Pullari (grazing-tax)/forest satyagraha led by Kanneganti Hanumanthu, martyred 1922.
Forms: no-tax campaigns, toddy-shop picketing, boycott of courts/councils/titles; ended after Chauri Chaura (Feb 1922).
items.source: Wikipedia — Non-Cooperation Movement; Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya; Kanneganti Hanumanthu

items.title: Chirala–Perala Satyagraha & Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya
items.body:
**In one line** — The story of a whole town that walked out of its homes rather than pay unfair taxes, led by the orator-poet 'Andhra Ratna'.

**Why it is asked** — The single word 'Ramnagar' and the title 'Andhra Ratna' are classic one-mark hooks; the episode is the model example of mass non-cooperation in Andhra.

## The story

- **Cause:** the twin towns of **Chirala and Perala** (Guntur district) were upgraded to **municipal status**. A municipality could levy higher taxes, so the residents' tax burden jumped sharply.
- **What happened (1921):** under **Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya**, the people decided that if living in a 'municipality' meant paying more, they would simply stop living in it. They **left the twin towns together** and built a camp of huts on the outskirts, naming it **Ramnagar**, where they stayed for about **eleven months**. With no residents, the municipality could collect no tax.
- **Result:** the protest became famous all over Andhra as a brilliant, peaceful way to defeat an unjust tax — a textbook case of **non-violent mass non-cooperation**.

## About the leader — 'Andhra Ratna'

- **Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya** was a **poet, singer, orator and Gandhian**, honoured as **Andhra Ratna** ('Jewel of Andhra').
- He was the **first Andhra leader to become a secretary of the All India Congress Committee (AICC)** — the Congress's top executive body.
- His powerful speeches and songs could gather and move huge crowds.

## Picture it

```
Chirala + Perala  --(taxes rise after 'municipality' status)-->  people leave
       |                                                              |
       +----------------->  live in hut-camp 'Ramnagar' (~11 months) --+
                                   municipality gets NO tax
```

## Terms explained

- **Municipality** — a town's local self-government body that can levy local taxes.
- **AICC (All India Congress Committee)** — the central executive committee of the Indian National Congress.
- **Andhra Ratna** — 'Jewel of Andhra', the honorific title of Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya.

**Don't confuse** — Chirala–Perala's special feature is the **Ramnagar exodus**, not a land-revenue refusal (that was Pedanandipadu) and not a grazing-tax fight (that was Palnadu).

**Remember it** — 'Duggirala = Andhra Ratna = the town that moved to Ramnagar.'

**TL;DR**

- Chirala & Perala upgraded to a municipality → higher taxes (1921).
- Residents left and lived in a hut-camp called **Ramnagar** for ~11 months.
- Leader: **Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya**, 'Andhra Ratna', first Andhra AICC secretary.
- A model of non-violent mass non-cooperation.
keyPoints: Chirala–Perala protested the towns' upgrade to a municipality and its higher taxes (1921).
Residents vacated the twin towns and lived in a hut-camp called 'Ramnagar' for ~11 months.
Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya led the satyagraha and was titled 'Andhra Ratna'.
He was the first Andhra leader to become an AICC secretary.
The agitation is a classic example of non-violent mass non-cooperation in Andhra.

items.title: Rampa (Manyam) Rebellion & Alluri Sitarama Raju (1922–24)
items.body:
**In one line** — An armed revolt of hill tribes in the Godavari forests, led by Alluri Sitarama Raju, against British forest laws and forced labour.

**Why it is asked** — The cause (1882 Forest Act), the leader's title ('Manyam Veerudu'), and the date of his death (7 May 1924) are the three facts examiners test.

## The story

- **Cause:** the **1882 Madras Forest Act** and the reserved-forest rules stopped the hill tribes from practising **podu** (shifting cultivation — clearing a forest patch, farming it a few years, then moving on) and from freely using forest produce. On top of this, the British forced the tribes into **vetti** (unpaid, forced labour) on roads and works. These two grievances destroyed the tribes' way of life.
- **What happened:** in the **Godavari agency** (the hill tracts called **Manyam**), **Alluri Sitarama Raju** organised the tribes into a fighting force. The revolt began in **August 1922**. Using **guerrilla tactics** (quick surprise attacks, then melting back into the forest), the rebels **raided police stations** — at **Chintapalle, Krishnadevipeta and Rajavommangi** — to seize guns and ammunition.
- **Result:** the British had to send in the **Malabar Special Police** to crush the rising. The rebellion ended when Raju was **captured and shot dead on 7 May 1924**. He is revered as **'Manyam Veerudu'** — Hero of the Jungle.

## Picture it (timeline)

| When | What |
|---|---|
| 1882 | Madras Forest Act curbs podu & forest use |
| Aug 1922 | Revolt begins; raids on police stations for arms |
| 1922–24 | Guerrilla war; British bring Malabar Special Police |
| 7 May 1924 | Alluri captured and shot — revolt ends |

## Terms explained

- **Podu** — shifting cultivation: clear a forest patch, farm it a few years, then move on.
- **Vetti (begar)** — unpaid, forced labour demanded by the authorities.
- **Agency / Manyam** — the hill and forest tracts of the Godavari region inhabited mainly by tribes.
- **Guerrilla tactics** — small, mobile surprise attacks rather than open battle.
- **Manyam Veerudu** — 'Hero of the Jungle', Alluri's popular title.

**Don't confuse** — the Rampa Rebellion was an **armed tribal revolt**, completely separate from the Gandhian, **non-violent** Non-Cooperation satyagrahas happening in coastal Andhra at the same time.

**Remember it** — 'Forest Act took their land → Alluri took up arms → fell on 7 May 1924.'

**TL;DR**

- Rampa/Manyam Rebellion: armed tribal revolt in the Godavari agency, Aug 1922 – May 1924.
- Cause: 1882 Madras Forest Act (podu curbs) + vetti (forced labour).
- Leader: Alluri Sitarama Raju, 'Manyam Veerudu'; guerrilla raids on police stations for arms.
- British used the Malabar Special Police; Alluri shot dead 7 May 1924.
keyPoints: Rampa/Manyam Rebellion (Aug 1922 – May 1924) was an armed tribal revolt in the Godavari agency.
Causes: 1882 Madras Forest Act curbing podu cultivation, plus forced labour (vetti/begar).
Led by Alluri Sitarama Raju, known as 'Manyam Veerudu'.
Guerrilla raids on police stations (Chintapalle, Krishnadevipeta, Rajavommangi) for arms.
Raju was captured and shot dead on 7 May 1924, ending the rebellion.
items.source: Wikipedia — Rampa Rebellion of 1922; Alluri Sitarama Raju

items.title: Civil Disobedience & Quit India in Andhra
items.body:
**In one line** — The two big final-phase movements — Salt Satyagraha (1930) and Quit India (1942) — and the forms they took along Andhra's coast.

**Why it is asked** — APPSC asks why salt satyagraha suited coastal Andhra, and what Quit India looked like once the leaders were jailed.

## The story

**Salt Satyagraha / Civil Disobedience (1930)**
- **Cause:** the British kept a monopoly and tax on salt. Gandhi's **Dandi March (1930)** broke this law by making salt from sea water, launching the **Civil Disobedience Movement** ('openly but peacefully break unjust laws').
- **What happened in Andhra:** Andhra has a long **eastern coastline**, so the natural form of protest was **making salt from sea water** and holding **coastal salt marches** along the **Krishna–Godavari and other coastal districts**.
- **Who led:** **Tanguturi Prakasam** — later called **'Andhra Kesari'** (Lion of Andhra) and famous for **baring his chest before the Simon Commission** in Madras (1928) — and other Congress leaders were active.

**Quit India Movement (1942)**
- **Cause:** frustrated by the lack of progress during World War II, the Congress demanded the British **'Quit India'**. Gandhi gave the call **'Do or Die'** on **8 August 1942** in Bombay.
- **What happened:** the British immediately jailed almost the entire Congress leadership. With no leaders to guide it, the movement became a **largely spontaneous, decentralised revolt** — in Andhra it meant **hartals (shutdowns), cutting communications, attacks on symbols of British authority, and mass arrests**.

## Picture it (timeline)

| Year | Movement | Andhra form |
|---|---|---|
| 1928 | Simon Commission | Prakasam bares his chest (Madras) |
| 1930 | Salt Satyagraha / Civil Disobedience | Coastal salt-making, Krishna–Godavari |
| 1942 | Quit India | Hartals, sabotage, mass arrests |

## Terms explained

- **Civil Disobedience** — openly but non-violently breaking unjust laws (e.g. the salt law).
- **Simon Commission (1928)** — an all-British commission on reforms, boycotted because it had no Indian members.
- **Andhra Kesari** — 'Lion of Andhra', the title of Tanguturi Prakasam.
- **Hartal** — a complete shutdown of shops and work as a form of protest.

**Don't confuse** — the **Simon Commission** (1928) and **Salt Satyagraha** (1930) are different events; Prakasam's chest-baring belongs to 1928, not the salt march.

**Remember it** — 'Coast → salt (1930); jailed leaders → spontaneous Quit India (1942).'

**TL;DR**

- Salt Satyagraha (1930): coastal salt-making along the Krishna–Godavari seaboard; Prakasam ('Andhra Kesari') prominent.
- Prakasam had bared his chest to the Simon Commission (1928).
- Quit India (1942): Gandhi's 'Do or Die' (8 Aug 1942); leaders jailed → spontaneous, decentralised revolt.
- Andhra 1942: hartals, attacks on British symbols, mass arrests.
keyPoints: Salt Satyagraha (1930) in Andhra used coastal salt-making along the Krishna–Godavari seaboard.
Tanguturi Prakasam ('Andhra Kesari') was prominent; he had bared his chest to the Simon Commission (1928).
Quit India began with Gandhi's 'Do or Die' call on 8 August 1942.
In Andhra, 1942 saw hartals, attacks on British symbols and large-scale arrests.
With leaders imprisoned, the 1942 movement was largely spontaneous and decentralised.
items.source: Wikipedia — Salt March; Quit India Movement; Tanguturi Prakasam

items.title: Andhra Leaders of the Freedom Struggle — Titles at a Glance
items.body:
**In one line** — A quick reference to the main Andhra freedom fighters, their honorific titles, and the one thing each is remembered for.

**Why it is asked** — Match-the-title questions (leader ↔ title) and 'who is known for X' are almost guaranteed, so the pairs must be over-learnt.

## The story

The Andhra freedom struggle was not the work of one kind of leader. It had an **armed tribal** strand (Alluri), a **peasant/town satyagraha** strand (Duggirala, Parvataneni, Kanneganti), an **organisational** strand (Konda Venkatappayya, Prakasam), and a **literary** strand (the poet Garimella and the strongman-symbol Kodi Rammurthy). Together these gave the movement its unusually broad base.

## Who was who

| Leader | Title | Chiefly known for |
|---|---|---|
| **Alluri Sitarama Raju** | Manyam Veerudu | Armed Rampa (Manyam) Rebellion, 1922–24 |
| **Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya** | Andhra Ratna | Chirala–Perala satyagraha; first Andhra AICC secretary |
| **Kanneganti Hanumanthu** | (Palnadu martyr) | Palnadu forest/Pullari satyagraha; martyred 1922 |
| **Konda Venkatappayya** | Desabhakta | Lawyer–Congress organiser of Non-Cooperation campaigns |
| **Tanguturi Prakasam** | Andhra Kesari | Defiance of the Simon Commission (1928); salt satyagraha |
| **Garimella Satyanarayana** | (nationalist poet) | Patriotic songs that mobilised the masses; jailed repeatedly |
| **Kodi Rammurthy Naidu** | (strongman) | Feats of strength symbolising national self-confidence |

## Terms explained

- **Manyam Veerudu** — 'Hero of the Jungle (hill tracts)'.
- **Andhra Ratna** — 'Jewel of Andhra'.
- **Desabhakta** — 'Patriot / devotee of the nation'.
- **Andhra Kesari** — 'Lion of Andhra'.

**Don't confuse** — keep the four titles straight: Raju = Manyam Veerudu, Duggirala = Andhra Ratna, Konda = Desabhakta, Prakasam = Andhra Kesari. The common trap is swapping Duggirala and Alluri, or Konda and Prakasam.

**Remember it** — 'Raju roars in the jungle (Veerudu); Duggirala is the Jewel; Konda the Patriot; Prakasam the Lion.'

**TL;DR**

- Alluri Sitarama Raju = Manyam Veerudu (Rampa Rebellion).
- Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya = Andhra Ratna (Chirala–Perala; first Andhra AICC secretary).
- Konda Venkatappayya = Desabhakta; Tanguturi Prakasam = Andhra Kesari.
- Kanneganti Hanumanthu = Palnadu martyr (1922); Garimella Satyanarayana = nationalist poet.
keyPoints: Alluri Sitarama Raju = 'Manyam Veerudu' (Rampa Rebellion).
Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya = 'Andhra Ratna' (Chirala–Perala).
Konda Venkatappayya = 'Desabhakta'; Tanguturi Prakasam = 'Andhra Kesari'.
Kanneganti Hanumanthu led and was martyred in the Palnadu satyagraha (1922).
Garimella Satyanarayana was the nationalist poet jailed for his patriotic songs.
items.mnemonic: Titles: Raju=Manyam Veerudu, Duggirala=Andhra Ratna, Konda=Desabhakta, Prakasam=Andhra Kesari.
items.source: Wikipedia — Alluri Sitarama Raju; Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya; Kanneganti Hanumanthu; Konda Venkatappayya; Tanguturi Prakasam; Garimella Satyanarayana

items.title: For Mains — Andhra in the Freedom Movement
items.body:
**In one line** — For Mains (Paper-II, AP Modern History clauses M2-8/M2-9), treat Andhra's freedom struggle as a *case study* of how national movements drew strength from local, regional and subaltern grievances.

**Why it is asked** — Paper-II explicitly lists 'Andhra nationalist movement' and the Andhra episodes of the national struggle; questions ask you to *analyse character and significance*, not just narrate events.

## Dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Causes | Colonial land-revenue pressure, forest laws (1882 Act), vetti, high municipal/grazing taxes, Swadeshi sentiment |
| Character | Dual nature — Gandhian non-violent satyagraha (coastal, peasant) **and** armed tribal militancy (Rampa) |
| Regional specificity | Why *coastal* Andhra did salt satyagraha; why the *agency* did an armed revolt |
| Social base | Peasants, forest tribes, small-town residents, poets, lawyers — unusually broad |
| Significance | Deepened Congress's rural roots; produced leaders; seeded the later separate-Andhra demand |
| Limitations | Localised, episodic; movements suspended from above (Chauri Chaura 1922); armed revolt crushed |

## Facts / episodes to quote

1. **Rampa Rebellion (1922–24)** — 1882 Madras Forest Act, podu, vetti; Alluri Sitarama Raju; raids on Chintapalle/Krishnadevipeta/Rajavommangi; shot 7 May 1924.
2. **Chirala–Perala (1921)** — Ramnagar exodus (~11 months) under Duggirala Gopalakrishnayya.
3. **Pedanandipadu no-tax (1921–22)** — Parvataneni Veerayya Choudary, guided by Konda Venkatappayya.
4. **Palnadu Pullari satyagraha** — Kanneganti Hanumanthu, martyred 1922.
5. **Hyderabad State** — Andhra Jana Sangham (1921) → Andhra Mahasabha (Jogipet, 1930, Suravaram Pratapa Reddy) as the Telugu, anti-Nizam strand (link to Praja Mandal / AISPC 1927).
6. **Civil Disobedience & Quit India** — coastal salt satyagraha (1930); Prakasam, 'Andhra Kesari'; 1942 hartals and sabotage.

## AP angle

Andhra is itself the 'AP angle' — stress that the region supplied the national movement with a **tribal-agrarian militancy** (Alluri) found in few other provinces, and that regional pride fed directly into the first **linguistic-states** demand after Independence.

## Use in answers

- **Example to cite:** contrast Chirala–Perala's peaceful exodus with Alluri's armed guerrilla war to show the movement's two faces in one sentence.
- **Quote idea:** describe Alluri as 'Manyam Veerudu' to signal the subaltern-tribal dimension.
- **Diagram idea:** a timeline bar (1905 Vandemataram → 1916 Home Rule → 1921 satyagrahas → 1922–24 Rampa → 1930 Salt → 1942 Quit India) to open or close the answer.

**TL;DR**

- Frame Andhra's struggle as 'national cause + local grievance', with a rare armed-tribal strand.
- Keep 5–6 datable episodes and their leaders ready to quote.
- End by linking regional pride to the later separate-Andhra/linguistic-states demand.
keyPoints: Mains clauses M2-8 (AP Modern) and M2-9 (Andhra nationalist movement), Paper-II.
Frame answers around causes · character (dual: Gandhian + armed-tribal) · social base · significance · limitations.
Quote 5–6 datable episodes: Rampa, Chirala–Perala, Pedanandipadu, Palnadu, Andhra Mahasabha, Salt/Quit India.
AP angle: tribal-agrarian militancy (Alluri) and the seed of the linguistic-states demand.
Use a timeline diagram and the 'Manyam Veerudu' subaltern framing in answers.
